children: Rising land costs and changing buyer preferences are pushing developers to reassess pricing, product mix and emerging residential corridors

Bengaluru’s residential market continued to grow in H1 2026, but rising unsold inventory and higher ticket sizes are creating pressure points beneath the headline expansion. Residential sales increased 5 per cent, while new launches rose 4 per cent during the period.

The gap between supply and absorption has become more visible, with around 35,000 units launched against roughly 28,000 sales and unsold inventory rising 22 per cent. At the same time, residential prices increased 9 per cent, raising questions around supply calibration, affordability and the sustainability of demand across different market segments.

Vivek Venkateswar, Director, SMP, Shriram Properties, said the increase in inventory needs to be viewed at a micro-market level. “This is not a city-wide phenomenon. Bengaluru launched approximately 35,000 units in H1 against roughly 28,000 sold, so the gap had to show up somewhere.”

The concentration of new projects within similar locations and price bands could, however, make absorption more challenging in select pockets if supply continues to build. “It sits in specific micro markets where several developers launched into the same price band within months of each other for example Hoskote,” Venkateswar said.
Premiumisation Tests Affordability

Bengaluru’s housing market is also moving towards higher ticket sizes, with Rs 1-2 crore homes accounting for 46 per cent of sales in H1 2026. Meanwhile, the Rs 2-5 crore segment has seen a sharp increase in launches, putting greater focus on whether premium supply is aligned with the size of the buyer pool.

Nesara BS, Chairman, Concorde, said the shift towards higher-value homes reflects changing buyer aspirations, but rising development costs are making lower-ticket housing harder to deliver in established locations. “As land and construction costs increase, delivering homes at lower ticket sizes in established locations becomes increasingly challenging.”

This could make the availability of housing across different price points increasingly important for maintaining broad-based absorption. “Bengaluru needs a diverse housing ecosystem across price points, because sustainable residential growth cannot depend only on the premium end of the market,” Nesara said.
North Growth Faces Infrastructure Challenge

North Bengaluru is emerging as a major residential expansion zone, with Devanahalli, Bagalur, Yelahanka and the Doddaballapur Road stretch gaining traction alongside the STRR. Airport connectivity, aerospace and hardware parks and the wider employment ecosystem are supporting the region’s growth, although infrastructure delivery remains a key variable.

Priyanka Raju, Director, Kalyani Developers, said the company’s focus on the region reflects its longer-term growth potential. “Micro-markets such as Devanahalli, Bagalur, Yelahanka and the Doddaballapur Road stretch, along with the STRR, continue to have significant room to grow, supported by the expanding employment ecosystem around the airport, aerospace and hardware parks.”

The broader expansion, however, is unlikely to remain concentrated in the north, as established employment centres and infrastructure continue to support other parts of the city. “At the same time, we see strong potential across South and East Bengaluru. Kanakapura Road has an established end-user base, social infrastructure and connectivity, while Whitefield and the eastern corridor continue to benefit from strong employment and infrastructure growth,” Raju said.
Prices Test Buyer Absorption

Bengaluru’s 9 per cent rise in residential prices during H1 2026 is adding another layer to the market’s affordability challenge. While sales continued to grow, the pace of price appreciation is raising questions about how much further buyers can absorb higher costs without becoming more selective or delaying purchase decisions.

Nesara said the relationship between pricing and affordability would increasingly differentiate individual projects and locations. “We expect pricing to become more differentiated across micro-markets rather than rise uniformly across the city.” He added that excessive pricing could lengthen buyer decision cycles.

That selectivity is also changing the emphasis for developers, as demand may increasingly depend on the perceived value delivered at a particular price point. Raju said, “The market is likely to move towards a more measured phase of price appreciation rather than continuing at the same pace indefinitely.”
Price Growth Faces Limits

The pressure becomes sharper when price growth is compared with income growth and the time required to absorb new housing supply. With sales up 5 per cent and prices rising 9 per cent in H1, a prolonged divergence between household purchasing capacity and property values could gradually affect absorption, particularly in higher-ticket segments.

Venkateswar said the current pace of appreciation is difficult to sustain against income growth. “Nine per cent price growth against mid-single digit income growth doesn't compound for long time and the strain amongst consumers is already visible.”

As the market adjusts, the correction may emerge through slower appreciation and developer-led incentives rather than an immediate reduction in quoted prices. “I would expect appreciation to settle at 5 to 6 per cent over the next 4 to 6 quarters, with the adjustment showing up in payment plans and inventory clearing offers rather than headline rates quoted by developers,” Venkateswar said.
